name: Treaty at Dent's and Vantine's Crossings (1851), unratified California treaty E
aka: Treaty E of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 4 set apart 'forever' for the sole use and occupancy of the signing tribes a district between the Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers, running eight miles along the Tuolumne, with ferries on the bounding rivers to be run by the agent for the tribes' benefit.
Additional Article 9 set apart a tract three miles square on the Tuolumne river below How's ferry for Captain Cornelius and his people.

Brood mares, milch cows, work cattle, mules, ploughs, harness and seed; a farmer with two assistants, a carpenter, a wheelwright, a blacksmith and school teachers, with school houses (Kappler, vol. 4, as excerpted by Oklahoma State University).

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty E in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 280, 281 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

plain.promised: A district between the Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers set apart forever, a tract three miles square for Captain Cornelius and his people, plus livestock, ploughs, seed, tradesmen and school teachers.
plain.happened: The Senate refused to ratify the treaty on July 8, 1852, and kept it secret until 1905. The tribes' lands were taken without the reserved tract or compensation.
plain.today: The treaty remains unratified. A 1928 Act let California Indians sue for the promised lands and compensation; the amount finally paid has not been traced. The Tuolumne Rancheria was bought for landless Indians in 1910, the Tribe's history says.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe counts itself among the parties to California's original unratified treaties, and its history says the Gold Rush destroyed the streams and gathering places that fed the Me-Wuk, that miners and militias commissioned by the federal government tried to control or wipe out the people, and that the Tuolumne Rancheria was bought for landless Indians only in 1910.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Buena Vista Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; California Valley Miwok Tribe, California; Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; Ione Band of Miwok Indians of California; Jackson Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; Middletown Rancheria of Pomo Indians of California; Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, Shingle Springs Rancheria (Verona Tract), California; Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians of the Tuolumne Rancheria of California.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

In Article 4 the signing tribes gave up their claims to other lands; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).

Audit 2026-11-08: promises corrected against treaty E as printed in Heizer (1972), the treaty text at https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366/files/arfs003-001.pdf; Heizer omits some of this treaty's articles, so the goods and staff are taken from Oklahoma State University's excerpt of Kappler vol. 4 (https://oms.library.okstate.edu/s/oklahoma-built/item/21826), and any subsistence (beef and flour) article was not checked; the earlier 'beef and flour during 1851 and 1852' line was removed because it was copied from the other treaties.
Status set to broken on 2026-11-08 under Jordan's rule: never ratified, but the land was taken and a finding documents it. The never-ratified breach stays so the map labels it.
